title: Is Graph Bipartite?
description:
There is an undirected graph with `n` nodes, where each node is numbered between `0` and `n - 1`. You are given a 2D array `graph`, where `graph[u]` is an array of nodes that node `u` is adjacent to.

A graph is bipartite if the nodes can be partitioned into two independent sets `A` and `B` such that every edge in the graph connects a node in set `A` and a node in set `B`.

Return `true` if and only if it is bipartite.
constraints: All the values of graph[u] are unique.
hints: A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd-length cycles.
Try to color the graph using 2 colors. Use BFS or DFS: assign color 0 to the starting node, and alternate colors for each neighbor.
If you ever try to assign a color to a node that is already colored with the same color as the current node, the graph is NOT bipartite.

title: Keys and Rooms
description:
There are `n` rooms labeled from `0` to `n - 1` and all the rooms are locked except for room `0`. Your goal is to visit all the rooms. However, you cannot enter a locked room without having its key.

When you visit a room, you may find a set of distinct keys in it. Each key has a number on it, denoting which room it unlocks, and you can take all of them with you to unlock the other rooms.

Given an array `rooms` where `rooms[i]` is the set of keys that you can get if you visited room `i`, return `true` if you can visit all the rooms, or `false` otherwise.
constraints: All values of rooms[i] are unique.
hints: Model this as a graph reachability problem — rooms are nodes, and keys are directed edges.
Start from room 0. Use DFS or BFS to explore all rooms reachable from the current set of keys.
Track which rooms have been visited. At the end, check if the count of visited rooms equals n.

title: Clone Graph
description:
Given a reference of a node in a connected undirected graph. Return a deep copy (clone) of the graph.

Each node in the graph contains a value (int) and a list (List[Node]) of its neighbors.

Test case format:

For simplicity, each node's value is the same as the node's index (1-indexed). For example, if `val = 1`, then it is the first node visited. So on and so forth. The graph is represented in the test case using an adjacency list.

An adjacency list `[ [2,4], [1,3], [2,4], [1,3] ]` represents the graph:

`1--2`
`|  |`
`4--3`

There are 4 nodes in total. Node 1 is connected to Node 2 and Node 4. Node 2 is connected to Node 1 and Node 3. Node 3 is connected to Node 2 and Node 4. Node 4 is connected to Node 1 and Node 3.
constraints: The number of nodes in the graph is in the range [0, 100].
Node.val is unique for each node.
There are no repeated edges and no self-loops in the graph.
The graph is connected and all nodes have unique values.
hints: Use a hash map to store visited nodes and their clones.
Traverse the graph using BFS or DFS.

title: Course Schedule

You are given an array `prerequisites` where `prerequisites[i] = [ai, bi]` indicates that you must take course `bi` first if you want to take course `ai`. For example, the pair `[0, 1]`, indicates that to take course `0` you have to first take course `1`.

Return `true` if you can finish all courses. Otherwise, return `false`.

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
description:
There is an `m x n` rectangular island that borders both the Pacific Ocean and Atlantic Ocean. The Pacific Ocean touches the island's left and top edges, and the Atlantic Ocean touches the island's right and bottom edges.

The island is partitioned into a grid of square cells. You are given an `m x n` integer matrix `heights` where `heights[r][c]` represents the height above sea level of the cell at coordinate `(r, c)`.

Water can flow from any cell `(r, c)` to an adjacent cell `(r', c')` if `heights[r'][c'] <= heights[r][c]`. Water can flow horizontally, vertically, and to all four directions.

Find the list of grid coordinates `(r, c)` where water can flow from `(r, c)` to both the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans.
hints: Instead of simulating water flow from every cell, try simulating water flow *into* cells from the oceans.
Use two separate BFS/DFS traversals, one starting from all cells bordering the Pacific, and another starting from all cells bordering the Atlantic.
A cell `(r, c)` is a valid answer if it's reachable by water from *both* oceans.

description:

`0` representing an empty cell,
`1` representing a fresh orange,

Every minute, any fresh orange that is 4-directionally adjacent to a rotten orange becomes rotten.

Return the minimum number of minutes that must elapse until no fresh oranges remain. If it is impossible to make every fresh orange rotten, return `-1`.

Use a queue to store all initially rotten oranges, and process them level by level.
Keep track of the time elapsed and the number of fresh oranges.
If any fresh oranges remain after the BFS completes, it's impossible.

title: Alien Dictionary
description:
There is a new alien language that uses the English alphabet. However, the order among the letters is unknown to you.
You are given a list of strings `words` from the alien language's dictionary, where the strings are sorted lexicographically by the rules of this new language.
Derive the order of the letters in this language. If there are multiple valid orderings, return any of them. If no ordering is possible, return an empty string.
It is guaranteed that all characters are lowercase English letters.
The dictionary may contain duplicate words. The order of characters is only determined by the first different character in two adjacent words.
constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Build a directed graph where an edge `u -> v` means `u` comes before `v`.
Find the topological sort of the graph.
Handle cycles (impossible ordering) and unreachable characters.

title: Word Ladder II
description:
A transformation sequence from `beginWord` to `endWord` using a dictionary `wordList` is a sequence of words `beginWord -> s1 -> s2 -> ... -> sk -> endWord` such that:
1. Every adjacent pair of words differs by a single letter.
2. Every `si` for `1 <= i <= k` is in `wordList`. Note that `beginWord` does not need to be in `wordList`.
3. `endWord` is in `wordList`.
Given two words, `beginWord` and `endWord`, and a dictionary `wordList`, return *all the shortest transformation sequences* from `beginWord` to `endWord`, or an empty list if no such sequence exists. If there are multiple shortest transformation sequences, return all of them.

Avoid cycles during path reconstruction by ensuring words are visited in increasing order of distance from `beginWord`.

title: Reconstruct Itinerary
description:

All of the tickets belong to a man who departs from `"JFK"`. Thus, the itinerary must begin with `"JFK"`.
If there are multiple valid itineraries, you should return the itinerary that has the smallest lexical order when read as a single string. For example, the itinerary `["JFK", "LGA"]` has a smaller lexical order than `["JFK", "LGB"]`.
All airports are represented by three uppercase English letters.
You may assume that there exists at least one valid itinerary. All tickets are used exactly once.

title: Path With Minimum Effort
description:
You are a hiker preparing for an upcoming trip. You are given `heights`, a 2D array of size `rows x columns`, where `heights[row][col]` represents the height of a cell.
You are initially located at `(0, 0)` and wish to reach the bottom-right cell `(rows - 1, columns - 1)`. You can move up, down, left, or right.
A path's *effort* is the maximum absolute difference in heights between two consecutive cells of the path.
Return the minimum *effort* required to travel from `(0, 0)` to `(rows - 1, columns - 1)`.
hints: This problem can be framed as finding a path from source to destination such that the maximum edge weight on the path is minimized. This is a classic "minimax" path problem.
Consider binary searching on the answer (the maximum effort). For a given `k` (max effort), can you reach the destination using only edges with effort <= `k`? Use BFS/DFS for this check.

Alternatively, adapt Dijkstra's algorithm. Instead of minimizing the sum of weights, minimize the maximum weight encountered so far. Use a priority queue to always explore the cell that can be reached with the minimum *current maximum effort*.
